Vaibhav, don't tear that sheet. Give it here. You know what this reminds me of? When I was twenty-five, new in this office, I started calligraphy in the evenings. I had pinned up photos of old Persian manuscripts above my table, and my letters looked like broken twigs next to them. I wanted to throw every page away.
My teacher said, 'Your eye is ahead of your hand. That's good. Keep everything.' So I did. Every evening's sheet went into a shoebox, date on the corner, even the ugly ones. Especially the ugly ones.
A year later I was clearing the shelf and opened that box. The first sheets made me cringe, and then laugh. Day by day I never saw it, but side by side it was plain. So, Vaibhav, date this one and keep it. Your Indu-ma'am is telling you.

qa.a: She kept every evening's sheet in a shoebox, with the date on the corner.

qa.a: She felt embarrassed and discouraged because her letters looked like broken twigs next to the manuscripts she admired.

qa.a: Indu chose to keep every evening's sheet in the box, even the ugly ones, and a year later the dated pages showed progress she never noticed day by day.

qa.a: The teacher saw them as a good sign that Indu's eye was ahead of her hand, not as a reason to quit.

Farida worked the late shift at the call centre, so her drawing happened in scraps: fifteen minutes on the staff bus, sometimes ten in the canteen. She had a cheap sketchbook and one pencil worn to a stub.
She loved the loose, lively portraits she saw in old illustrated books. Her own faces came out stiff, eyes too big, noses like triangles. Some nights she nearly closed the book for good.
Instead she made one small habit. Every sketch, however bad, got photographed and dropped into a folder on her phone called 'awful but dated'.
In April her friend Nandini was scrolling through it while they waited for the bus. 'Wait, this is from November?' She held the phone next to the latest one. The first face was a mask. The newest one was almost smiling.
Farida stared at them for a long time.

qa.q: What did Farida call the folder on her phone?
qa.a: She called the folder 'awful but dated'.

qa.q: What might Farida have been thinking as she stared at the two drawings for a long time?
qa.a: She was probably taking in, with surprise and some pride, that she had improved far more than she had felt day to day.

qa.q: Which habit helped Farida get through the stiff, awkward stage, and why?
qa.a: Photographing every sketch with its date let her keep going despite the ugly ones, and later gave clear proof of progress.

qa.q: What is it like for Nandini to see the two drawings side by side?
qa.a: Nandini is surprised and pleased, and gets to show her friend something Farida couldn't see on her own.

grounding: It shows an adult learner with little time accepting the awkward stage, keeping a dated record, and later seeing progress hidden in daily practice.

Rajni's first watercolour of the Bandra sea looked like dishwater. She knew it; she had spent years in galleries and could see exactly how far it was from what she wanted. Her flatmate Neelam found her about to tear it in half.
"Don't," Neelam said. "Date it and keep it."
Rajni grumbled, but she started a folder anyway. Every Sunday one painting went in, however ugly, with the date on the back in pencil. She stopped holding each one up against the paintings in her head and simply painted the next.
In March, clearing the cupboard, she opened the folder and laid the pages out on the floor in order. The first still made her wince. By the tenth, the sky had a gradient. By the twentieth, the water looked wet.
"I didn't see this happening," she said.
Neelam leaned in the doorway. "Nobody sees it from inside."

qa.q: What did Rajni write on the back of each painting?
qa.a: The date, in pencil.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel when she laid the pages out on the floor?
qa.a: She felt surprised and quietly proud, seeing progress she had never noticed from week to week.

qa.q: Which habit helped Rajni through the awkward stage, and why?
qa.a: Keeping every Sunday painting dated in a folder; seeing the whole set together showed growth that weekly painting hid.

qa.q: How does Neelam see Rajni's struggle?
qa.a: Neelam sees the ugly early paintings as a normal stage and gently stops Rajni from tearing them up.

grounding: A young adult painter accepts her awkward early work, keeps dated records and later sees progress that week-to-week practice hid.

"It smells amazing, though."
"Smell doesn't count. I've eaten bread from real bakeries, I know what it should look like. Mine looks like a doorstop."
"So stop?"

"Because the teacher at the baking workshop said the clumsy months are normal, and in two months I'll forget how bad I started."
Nine weeks later:
"Rehana! Come here. Scroll with me."
"Brick, brick, pancake... wait, that one has holes."

"That's actual bread, Jahnavi."
"I didn't notice it getting better. I only see it now, all together."

When I started writing stories at twenty-five, I already knew good writing. I'd read hundreds of books. That was the problem: every sentence I wrote sounded like a school essay next to them, and I wanted to delete everything.
Joseph, who runs our Thursday writing circle, told me not to. "Put it all in a folder called Bad Drafts, Divyansh. Don't open it for a year."
It felt silly, but I did it. I kept writing one story a month and kept dropping the early versions into that folder.
Last week, a year and a bit later, I opened it. Story one had nine adjectives in the first line. I read it out to myself and laughed. Then I read my latest. It isn't great, but it breathes.
I couldn't feel that change while it was happening. The folder could. I'm keeping it.

qa.q: What was the folder called?
qa.a: Bad Drafts.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel about writing at the start?
qa.a: Divyansh felt embarrassed and discouraged, since every sentence sounded like a school essay next to the books already read.

qa.q: Which choice helped Divyansh get past the awkward stage?
qa.a: Keeping every early draft in a folder instead of deleting it, then comparing a year later, which showed real progress.

qa.q: What might Joseph have known that Divyansh didn't at the start?
qa.a: Joseph probably knew from experience that beginners can't see their own progress, so a saved record would reassure Divyansh later.

grounding: A young writer accepts the awkward stage, keeps early drafts and later sees progress that month-to-month writing hid.

Calligraphy class note, evening batch, 12 March.
Noor, our newest adult student, brought her folder tonight. In January she almost quit: she said her letters looked nothing like the old manuscripts she loves, and she hated every page. I suggested she keep every attempt, even the ugly ones, dated, in one folder, and not judge them for three months. Tonight I asked her to lay her first page next to tonight's. She went quiet. Then she laughed. The January alif leaned like a tired tree; tonight's stood straight. "I didn't see it happening," she said. "Every day it just felt awkward." I told her the awkward feeling is what learning feels like from the inside. She wants to keep the folder going. I will ask her to compare again in June.
Farhan

qa.q: What did Noor lay side by side tonight?
qa.a: Her first page from January and tonight's page.

qa.q: What did Noor feel on seeing the two pages side by side?
qa.a: She went quiet, then laughed, surprised and pleased to see progress she had not felt day to day.

qa.q: Why was the dated folder a useful practice?
qa.a: It made visible the progress that daily practice hides, and helped Noor accept the awkward stage instead of quitting.

qa.q: What might Farhan feel watching Noor laugh?
qa.a: Farhan likely feels glad and satisfied, having encouraged her through the January urge to quit.

grounding: Shows an adult learner accepting the awkward stage and keeping dated early attempts, so looking back reveals progress hidden day to day.
